function.name: cronjob
function.description:
Manage scheduled cron jobs with a single compressed tool.

Use action='create' to schedule a new job from a prompt or one or more skills.
Use action='list' to inspect jobs.
Use action='update', 'pause', 'resume', 'remove', or 'run' to manage an existing job.

To stop a job the user no longer wants: first action='list' to find the job_id, then action='remove' with that job_id. Never guess job IDs — always list first.

Jobs run in a fresh session with no current-chat context, so prompts must be self-contained.
If skills are provided on create, the future cron run loads those skills in order, then follows the prompt as the task instruction.
On update, passing skills=[] clears attached skills.

NOTE: The agent's final response is auto-delivered to the target. Put the primary
user-facing content in the final response. Cron jobs run autonomously with no user
present — they cannot ask questions or request clarification.

Important safety rule: cron-run sessions should not recursively schedule more cron jobs.

action.description: One of: create, list, update, pause, resume, remove, run

prompt.description: For create: the full self-contained prompt. If skills are also provided, this becomes the task instruction paired with those skills.

repeat.description: Optional repeat count. Omit for defaults (once for one-shot, forever for recurring).

deliver.description: Omit this parameter to auto-deliver back to the current chat and topic (recommended). Auto-detection preserves thread/topic context. Only set explicitly when the user asks to deliver somewhere OTHER than the current conversation. Values: 'origin' (same as omitting), 'local' (no delivery, save only), or platform:chat_id:thread_id for a specific destination. Examples: 'telegram:-1001234567890:17585', 'discord:#engineering', 'sms:+15551234567'. WARNING: 'platform:chat_id' without :thread_id loses topic targeting.

skills.description: Optional ordered list of skill names to load before executing the cron prompt. On update, pass an empty array to clear attached skills.

model.description: Optional per-job model override. If provider is omitted, the current main provider is pinned at creation time so the job stays stable.

provider.description: Provider name (e.g. 'openrouter', 'anthropic'). Omit to use and pin the current provider.

script.description: Optional path to a Python script that runs before each cron job execution. Its stdout is injected into the prompt as context. Use for data collection and change detection. Relative paths resolve under ~/.hermes/scripts/. On update, pass empty string to clear.

context_from.description: Optional job ID or list of job IDs whose most recent completed output is injected into the prompt as context before each run. Use this to chain cron jobs: job A collects data, job B processes it. Each entry must be a valid job ID (from cronjob action='list'). Note: injects the most recent completed output — does not wait for upstream jobs running in the same tick. On update, pass an empty array to clear.

enabled_toolsets.description: Optional list of toolset names to restrict the job's agent to (e.g. ["web", "terminal", "file", "delegation"]). When set, only tools from these toolsets are loaded, significantly reducing input token overhead. When omitted, all default tools are loaded. Infer from the job's prompt — e.g. use "web" if it calls web_search, "terminal" if it runs scripts, "file" if it reads files, "delegation" if it calls delegate_task. On update, pass an empty array to clear.

workdir.description: Optional absolute path to run the job from. When set, AGENTS.md / CLAUDE.md / .cursorrules from that directory are injected into the system prompt, and the terminal/file/code_exec tools use it as their working directory — useful for running a job inside a specific project repo. Must be an absolute path that exists. When unset (default), preserves the original behaviour: no project context files, tools use the scheduler's cwd. On update, pass an empty string to clear. Jobs with workdir run sequentially (not parallel) to keep per-job directories isolated.

function.name: session_search
function.description:
Search your long-term memory of past conversations, or browse recent sessions. This is your recall -- every past session is searchable, and this tool summarizes what happened.

TWO MODES:
1. Recent sessions (no query): Call with no arguments to see what was worked on recently. Returns titles, previews, and timestamps. Zero LLM cost, instant. Start here when the user asks what were we working on or what did we do recently.
2. Keyword search (with query): Search for specific topics across all past sessions. Returns LLM-generated summaries of matching sessions.

USE THIS PROACTIVELY when:
- The user says 'we did this before', 'remember when', 'last time', 'as I mentioned'
- The user asks about a topic you worked on before but don't have in current context
- The user references a project, person, or concept that seems familiar but isn't in memory
- You want to check if you've solved a similar problem before
- The user asks 'what did we do about X?' or 'how did we fix Y?'

Don't hesitate to search when it is actually cross-session -- it's fast and cheap. Better to search and confirm than to guess or ask the user to repeat themselves.

Search syntax: keywords joined with OR for broad recall (elevenlabs OR baseten OR funding), phrases for exact match ("docker networking"), boolean (python NOT java), prefix (deploy*). IMPORTANT: Use OR between keywords for best results — FTS5 defaults to AND which misses sessions that only mention some terms. If a broad OR query returns nothing, try individual keyword searches in parallel. Returns summaries of the top matching sessions.

query.description: Search query — keywords, phrases, or boolean expressions to find in past sessions. Omit this parameter entirely to browse recent sessions instead (returns titles, previews, timestamps with no LLM cost).

role_filter.description: Optional: only search messages from specific roles (comma-separated). E.g. 'user,assistant' to skip tool outputs.

function.name: skill_manage
function.description:
Manage skills (create, update, delete). Skills are your procedural memory — reusable approaches for recurring task types. New skills go to ~/.hermes/skills/; existing skills can be modified wherever they live.

Actions: create (full SKILL.md + optional category), patch (old_string/new_string — preferred for fixes), edit (full SKILL.md rewrite — major overhauls only), delete, write_file, remove_file.

Create when: complex task succeeded (5+ calls), errors overcome, user-corrected approach worked, non-trivial workflow discovered, or user asks you to remember a procedure.
Update when: instructions stale/wrong, OS-specific failures, missing steps or pitfalls found during use. If you used a skill and hit issues not covered by it, patch it immediately.

After difficult/iterative tasks, offer to save as a skill. Skip for simple one-offs. Confirm with user before creating/deleting.

Good skills: trigger conditions, numbered steps with exact commands, pitfalls section, verification steps. Use skill_view() to see format examples.

name.description: Skill name (lowercase, hyphens/underscores, max 64 chars). Must match an existing skill for patch/edit/delete/write_file/remove_file.

content.description: Full SKILL.md content (YAML frontmatter + markdown body). Required for 'create' and 'edit'. For 'edit', read the skill first with skill_view() and provide the complete updated text.

old_string.description: Text to find in the file (required for 'patch'). Must be unique unless replace_all=true. Include enough surrounding context to ensure uniqueness.

new_string.description: Replacement text (required for 'patch'). Can be empty string to delete the matched text.

replace_all.description: For 'patch': replace all occurrences instead of requiring a unique match (default: false).

function.name: terminal
function.description:
Execute shell commands on a Linux environment. Filesystem usually persists between calls.

Do NOT use cat/head/tail to read files — use read_file instead.
Do NOT use grep/rg/find to search — use search_files instead.
Do NOT use ls to list directories — use search_files(target='files') instead.
Do NOT use sed/awk to edit files — use patch instead.
Do NOT use echo/cat heredoc to create files — use write_file instead.
Reserve terminal for: builds, installs, git, processes, scripts, network, package managers, and anything that needs a shell.

Foreground (default): Commands return INSTANTLY when done, even if the timeout is high. Set timeout=300 for long builds/scripts — you'll still get the result in seconds if it's fast. Prefer foreground for short commands.
Background: Set background=true to get a session_id. Two patterns:
  (1) Long-lived processes that never exit (servers, watchers).
  (2) Long-running tasks with notify_on_complete=true — you can keep working on other things and the system auto-notifies you when the task finishes. Great for test suites, builds, deployments, or anything that takes more than a minute.
For servers/watchers, do NOT use shell-level background wrappers (nohup/disown/setsid/trailing '&') in foreground mode. Use background=true so Hermes can track lifecycle and output.
After starting a server, verify readiness with a health check or log signal, then run tests in a separate terminal() call. Avoid blind sleep loops.
Use process(action="poll") for progress checks, process(action="wait") to block until done.
Working directory: Use 'workdir' for per-command cwd.
PTY mode: Set pty=true for interactive CLI tools (Codex, Claude Code, Python REPL).

Do NOT use vim/nano/interactive tools without pty=true — they hang without a pseudo-terminal. Pipe git output to cat if it might page.

command.description: The command to execute on the VM

background.description: Run the command in the background. Two patterns: (1) Long-lived processes that never exit (servers, watchers). (2) Long-running tasks paired with notify_on_complete=true — you can keep working and get notified when the task finishes. For short commands, prefer foreground with a generous timeout instead.

timeout.description: Max seconds to wait (default: 180, foreground max: 600). Returns INSTANTLY when command finishes — set high for long tasks, you won't wait unnecessarily. Foreground timeout above 600s is rejected; use background=true for longer commands.

workdir.description: Working directory for this command (absolute path). Defaults to the session working directory.

pty.description: Run in pseudo-terminal (PTY) mode for interactive CLI tools like Codex, Claude Code, or Python REPL. Only works with local and SSH backends. Default: false.

notify_on_complete.description: When true (and background=true), you'll be automatically notified exactly once when the process finishes. **This is the right choice for almost every long-running task** — tests, builds, deployments, multi-item batch jobs, anything that takes over a minute and has a defined end. Use this and keep working on other things; the system notifies you on exit. MUTUALLY EXCLUSIVE with watch_patterns — when both are set, watch_patterns is dropped.

watch_patterns.description: Strings to watch for in background process output. HARD RATE LIMIT: at most 1 notification per 15 seconds per process — matches arriving inside the cooldown are dropped. After 3 consecutive 15-second windows with dropped matches, watch_patterns is automatically disabled for that process and promoted to notify_on_complete behavior (one notification on exit, no more mid-process spam). USE ONLY for truly rare, one-shot mid-process signals on LONG-LIVED processes that will never exit on their own — e.g. ['Application startup complete'] on a server so you know when to hit its endpoint, or ['migration done'] on a daemon. DO NOT use for: (1) end-of-run markers like 'DONE'/'PASS' — use notify_on_complete instead; (2) error patterns like 'ERROR'/'Traceback' in loops or multi-item batch jobs — they fire on every iteration and you'll hit the strike limit fast; (3) anything you'd ever combine with notify_on_complete. When in doubt, choose notify_on_complete. MUTUALLY EXCLUSIVE with notify_on_complete — set one, not both.

*Finding love in the space between atoms*

### The Graduate Engineer

Fermilab in 1970 was a place of contradictions—a frontier outpost of pure science planted in the cornfields west of Chicago, where the world's most sophisticated technology coexisted with rural Illinois practicality. The main accelerator ring tunneled beneath farmland that had been cornfields just a few years before. Physicists in tweed jackets walked past equipment sheds where local farmers stored their harvest equipment. The frontier between cutting-edge research and agricultural tradition ran through every aspect of daily life.

The work was everything he had hoped for and more challenging than he had expected. Fermilab's control systems were a patchwork of technologies—some state-of-the-art, some obsolete the day they were installed, all needing to work together with absolute reliability. A particle accelerator is a delicate instrument. The beam travels at nearly the speed of light through a vacuum pipe surrounded by superconducting magnets operating at temperatures near absolute zero. Thousands of sensors monitor every parameter, and the control systems Bob worked on had to process this data in real time, making adjustments faster than human operators could react.

I spent my days in a windowless control room buried beneath the Illinois prairie, surrounded by racks of electronics that hummed and clicked like living things. The air smelled of ozone and solder and the faint chemical tang of cooling systems. When a problem surfaced—and they always surfaced—I'd trace the fault through miles of cable, through schematics that unfolded across conference tables, through the accumulated knowledge of engineers who had built this place from scratch. There was something sacred about it: the knowledge that the beam passing through these magnets was doing what no human eye had ever seen, revealing the architecture of matter itself. And I was part of the infrastructure that made that possible.

The job had one flaw. It was an eighteen-month contract: design and build an instrument, hand it to the scientists, and then the job was over. The grant money ended. When the final handoff came, I felt a hollow satisfaction. The system worked beautifully. But it belonged to someone else now. I packed up my desk, walked past the cornfields one last time, and drove away wondering what came next.

### The Change

After the lab job ended, Bob was looking for work. The economy was slowing and jobs were scarce. He interviewed in California and Washington but found a job with a Michigan company working as a flight test engineer in Florida at Eglin Air Force Base, developing and testing software on a reconnaissance jet.

The transition was jarring. At Fermilab, the culture was academic—professorial, collaborative, unhurried. At Eglin, everything moved at the speed of jet exhaust. Briefings started at 0500. Coffee was a utility, not a luxury. The men around me wore flight suits and carried the quiet confidence of people who had pushed machines to their limits and lived to tell about it. They spoke a language of sorties and flight envelopes and g-forces, and for the first few weeks I struggled to keep up.

I remember the first time I climbed into the back seat of an RF-4C Phantom. The cockpit was tight, everything within arm's reach, switches and dials packed so densely it felt like sitting inside a circuit diagram. The canopy sealed shut with a thud that cut off the outside world, leaving only the hum of electronics and the faint chemical smell of hydraulic fluid. When the engines spooled up, the vibration went straight through the seat into my spine. The takeoff pushed me into the seatback with a force I had never felt—four tons of thrust, raw and immediate, the runway blurring beneath us until the ground fell away and the Florida coastline tilted sideways through the canopy. I was a civilian contractor, and by all rights I shouldn't have been in that seat. But the pilots trusted me. They wanted me to understand what the systems felt like, not just what the data said. That trust was earned over months of late nights, of being the first one in and the last one out, of fixing problems before they were asked about. It was the best kind of education, the kind you can't get from a textbook.

### London

The first time I went to London, I was twenty-seven years old, young, American, and convinced that the world was my oyster. I had a company expense account, guidebooks, and a head full of notions about what awaited. London taught me otherwise. Within the first hour, it dismantled every assumption I ever had about myself.

I stepped off the plane at Heathrow feeling invincible. This was it—the moment my adventure began, that legendary place where English was supposedly spoken but turned out to be a completely different language than the one I learned in school. But within an hour of leaving the airport, I was lost. My accent was wrong. My clothes were wrong. My entire way of moving through the world was wrong.

"Excuse me," I asked a passing stranger, "could you tell me how to get to the subway station?" The correct word was *tube*. He looked at me—really looked at me—and I saw something in his eyes that I hadn't encountered before. It wasn't hostility, exactly. It was something subtler. Dismissal. Mild contempt. The quiet judgment of someone who saw me as an ignorant American, another wide-eyed tourist who didn't understand that the world didn't revolve around them. "Tube's that way," he said, pointing in a direction that seemed to contradict what my map said, and walked away without another word.

The first week was humbling. I made mistake after mistake, each one a small embarrassment that added up to a profound lesson in humility. I asked for "chips" and received what I would have called "fries." I asked for "pants" and nearly caused a shop assistant to blush. I tried to compliment a coworker's outfit and received a look of confusion—the words meant something different here. There were moments of genuine loneliness. I would sit in my Victorian hotel room, surrounded by travelers from a dozen different countries, and wonder what the hell I was doing there.

I learned to love the pubs with their dark wood and warm beer—warm, yes, but somehow comforting in a way I never expected. I learned to navigate the Underground like a native, memorizing which lines connected where, understanding the peculiar etiquette of standing on the right and walking on the left.

I made friends. Actual friends, among my coworkers and counterparts. They showed me the London they knew: the tucked-away cafes where the coffee was better than anything I'd had in America, the street markets where you could find anything if you looked hard enough, the parks where Londoners escaped the chaos of the city to read, relax, and pretend they weren't in one of the busiest places on Earth. ### Nancy

I met Nancy in a grocery store in Michigan, on one of those trips home between flight test rotations. I was standing near the eggs—I remember that detail with absurd clarity, the way you remember the trivial things that frame the moments that change your life—when I noticed the woman next to me, studying the price tag with an expression of genuine outrage.

"Can you believe these prices?" I said, because I had to say something, and I'd been reading about inflation on the news. "Eggs are up, what, a hundred percent?"

She looked at me. Not the quick glance of polite dismissal, but a real look, appraising and amused. "You're not from here," she said. It wasn't a question.

"How can you tell?"

"What are the odds?" I said.

"In a town this size?" she replied. "Pretty good, actually. But I'll pretend to be surprised."

I asked her out. She said yes.

I remembered my mother's advice, offered during a phone call when I had complained about feeling out of place: "You don't have to be the smartest person in the room, Bobby. You just have to be the most real. People remember that."

She worked at a bank, in the trust department, but what she really wanted to do was write. Novels, maybe. Stories, definitely. Her eyes lit up when she talked about it in a way they didn't when she talked about trusts and estates. Her ex-fiancé had called her literary ambitions frivolous. When she told me that, I saw a shadow cross her face—old hurt, still healing.

"That's not frivolous," I said. "Creating something out of words, making people feel things they didn't know they could feel—that's harder than anything I've ever done."

She looked at me for a long moment. "You mean that."

"I do."

### Courtship

The second date was easier. The third was comfortable. By the fourth, we were finishing each other's sentences, laughing at jokes no one else would understand—that particular intimacy that emerges when two people recognize in each other something they didn't know they were seeking. I told her about my family: the father who didn't always know how to be soft, the mother who taught me to see past the yelling, the lessons whispered in small moments that had shaped everything I became. Nancy told me about her failed engagement, the man who had wanted her to be someone she wasn't, who had seen her writing as a hobby rather than a calling.

There was a moment I still carry with me. We were walking through a park near her apartment, late autumn, the leaves piled gold and red along the path. She stopped to look at a maple tree, the branches almost bare against a gray Michigan sky. "I used to think I knew what my life would look like," she said quietly. "A house. A husband. A writing desk by a window. But the house and the husband were the wrong ones. The desk was the only part I got right." She turned to me. "What do you think your life looks like?"

I didn't have an answer. Not a good one. But the question stayed with me, and the fact that she asked it—that she wanted to know—told me more about who she was than any biography could. She wasn't looking for a man to complete her picture. She was looking for someone to share the blank page.

The night before I had to fly back to Florida, we sat in her apartment drinking wine and listening to a jazz station on the radio. We weren't talking about anything important. And yet. I looked at her across the small table, lamplight catching the curve of her face, the way she tapped her fingers in time with the music, and I knew. Not with my head. With something deeper. The kind of knowing that doesn't need proof.

"This is going to be a long-distance thing for a while," I said. "Are you okay with that?"

She took a sip of her wine. "I'm okay with it if you are."

"I'm more than okay with it."

### Building a Life

We were married in the spring, a small ceremony in Michigan with Nancy's family and my parents making awkward small talk across the cultural divide that separated their worlds. My father stood stiff in his good suit, looking uncomfortable but proud. My mother cried, as mothers do. Nancy wore a simple white dress and looked at me like I was the only person in the room.

We bought a small house in Michigan with me commuting to Florida. It was the first time either of us had lived with another adult in a romantic partnership, and the learning curve was steep. I had to adjust to sharing space, to considering another person's preferences, to the give-and-take of domestic life. Nancy had to adjust to my long hours, my tendency to become absorbed in technical problems, my occasional withdrawal when work was frustrating. We fought, as all couples do. About small things—whose turn it was to do dishes, whether to spend money on new furniture or save for the future. About larger things—whether I was working too much, whether Nancy was too quick to accommodate my schedule at the expense of her own needs.

What I remember most from those early years was the feeling of partnership. When I succeeded at work—a difficult problem solved, a system improved—Nancy celebrated with me, understood why it mattered, made my victories feel real. When I struggled, she offered perspective, reminded me that my worth wasn't measured by professional achievement, held me when the weight of expectation felt overwhelming. And I tried to do the same for her.

"You're allowed to be obsessed with your work," Nancy told me once, after I apologized for talking about a technical problem through dinner. "I just need to know that I'm also important. That when it really matters, you'll be there."

"You matter more than the work," I said. "I sometimes forget to show it. But you matter more."

It was true, though the balance was hard to maintain. I loved the work—loved the challenge, the sense of contributing to something larger than myself, the intellectual satisfaction of solving problems that had stumped others. But Nancy was my anchor, my connection to a world beyond the abstract realm of engineering and management. She reminded me that the purpose of technology was to serve people, that the work was less important than the humans, that my worth wasn't measured in technical achievements.

### The First Home

We bought our first house—a modest ranch in Michigan, close enough to the airport for my commute but in a town with good schools and a growing community. The house needed work. I approached it as an engineering project, creating plans, working weekends to transform the place into something we could be proud of.

"This is what my life has taught me," I said one Sunday evening, sitting on our newly finished deck with beers in hand, admiring the work. "Not just the skills, but the feeling. Making something better. Building something together."

We were young, then, and optimistic, and in love. We believed we had time—time to build careers, raise children, achieve dreams, grow old together. We didn't know how little time we actually had, how quickly the future we were building would be changed by forces we couldn't anticipate. But that knowledge was still years away.

Fermilab in 1970 was a place of contradictions—a frontier outpost of pure science planted in the cornfields west of Chicago, where the world's most sophisticated technology coexisted with rural Illinois practicality. The main accelerator ring tunneled beneath farmland that had been cornfields just a few years before. Physicists in tweed jackets walked past equipment sheds where local farmers stored their harvest equipment. The frontier between cutting-edge research and agricultural tradition ran through every aspect of daily life.

Bob arrived, fresh from graduation, carrying everything he owned in a used car with 120,000 miles on the odometer. His apartment in Batavia was small—one bedroom, kitchenette, bathroom the size of a closet—but it was his, paid for with his own salary.

The work was everything he had hoped for and more challenging than he had expected. Fermilab's control systems were a patchwork of technologies—some state-of-the-art, some obsolete the day they were installed, all needing to work together with absolute reliability. A particle accelerator is a delicate instrument. The beam travels at nearly the speed of light through a vacuum pipe surrounded by superconducting magnets operating at temperatures near absolute zero. Thousands of sensors monitor every parameter, and the control systems Bob worked on had to process this data in real time, making adjustments faster than human operators could react.

I spent my days in a windowless control room beneath the Illinois prairie, surrounded by racks of electronics that hummed and clicked like living things. The air smelled of ozone and solder and the faint chemical tang of cooling systems. When a problem surfaced, I'd trace the fault through miles of cable, through schematics that unfolded across conference tables, through the accumulated knowledge of engineers who had built this place from scratch. There was something sacred about it: the beam passing through these magnets was doing what no human eye had ever seen, revealing the architecture of matter itself. And I was part of the infrastructure that made that possible.

The job had one flaw. It was an eighteen-month contract: design and build an instrument, hand it to the scientists, and then it was over. The grant money ended. When the final handoff came, I felt a hollow satisfaction. The system worked beautifully. But it belonged to someone else now. I packed my desk, walked past the cornfields one last time, and drove away wondering what came next.

### The Change

After the lab job ended, Bob was looking for work. The economy was slowing and jobs were scarce. He interviewed in California and Washington but found a job with a Michigan company working as a flight test engineer in Florida at Eglin Air Force Base, developing and testing software on a reconnaissance jet.

The transition was jarring. At Fermilab, the culture was academic—professorial, collaborative, unhurried. At Eglin, everything moved at the speed of jet exhaust. Briefings started at 0500. Coffee was a utility, not a luxury. The men around me wore flight suits and carried the quiet confidence of people who had pushed machines to their limits and lived to tell about it. They spoke a language of sorties and flight envelopes and g-forces, and for the first few weeks I struggled to keep up.

I remember the first time I climbed into the back seat of an RF-4C Phantom. The cockpit was tight, everything within reach, switches and dials packed so densely it felt like sitting inside a circuit diagram. The canopy sealed shut with a thud that cut off the outside world, leaving only the hum of electronics and the faint chemical smell of hydraulic fluid. When the engines spooled up, the vibration went straight through the seat into my spine. The takeoff pushed me into the seatback with a force I had never felt—four tons of thrust, raw and immediate, the runway blurring beneath us until the ground fell away and the Florida coastline tilted sideways through the canopy. I was a civilian contractor, not supposed to be in that seat. But the pilots trusted me. They wanted me to feel what the systems felt like, not just read the data. That trust was earned over months of late nights, of being the first one in and the last one out, of fixing problems before they were asked about. The best kind of education, the kind you can't get from a textbook.

### London

The first time I went to London, I was twenty-seven years old, young, American, and convinced that the world was my oyster. I had a company expense account, guidebooks, and a head full of notions about what awaited. London taught me otherwise. Within the first hour, it dismantled every assumption I ever had about myself.

I stepped off the plane at Heathrow feeling invincible. This was it—the moment my adventure began, that legendary place where English was supposedly spoken but turned out to be a completely different language than the one I learned in school. But within an hour of leaving the airport, I was lost. My accent was wrong. My clothes were wrong. My entire way of moving through the world was wrong.

"Excuse me," I asked a passing stranger, "could you tell me how to get to the subway station?" The correct word was *tube*. He looked at me—really looked at me—and I saw something in his eyes that I hadn't encountered before. It wasn't hostility, exactly. It was something subtler. Dismissal. Mild contempt. The quiet judgment of someone who saw me as an ignorant American, another wide-eyed tourist who didn't understand that the world didn't revolve around them. "Tube's that way," he said, pointing in a direction that seemed to contradict what my map said, and walked away without another word.

The first week was humbling. I made mistake after mistake, each one a small embarrassment that added up to a profound lesson in humility. I asked for "chips" and received what I would have called "fries." I asked for "pants" and nearly caused a shop assistant to blush. I tried to compliment a coworker's outfit and received a look of confusion—the words meant something different here. There were moments of genuine loneliness. I would sit in my Victorian hotel room, surrounded by travelers from a dozen different countries, and wonder what the hell I was doing there.

But here's the thing about London: it grows on you. The more time I spent there, the more I understood its rhythms, its quirks, its secret beauty. I learned to love the pubs with their dark wood and warm beer—warm, yes, but somehow comforting in a way I never expected. I learned to navigate the Underground like a native, memorizing which lines connected where, understanding the peculiar etiquette of standing on the right and walking on the left.

I made friends. Actual friends, among my coworkers and counterparts. They showed me the London they knew: the tucked-away cafes where the coffee was better than anything I'd had in America, the street markets where you could find anything if you looked hard enough, the parks where Londoners escaped the chaos of the city to read, relax, and pretend they weren't in one of the busiest places on Earth. I returned to London many times since then. Each visit, I discover something new. The city is like that—it keeps secrets, reveals them slowly, rewards patience. And that's a lesson I carried with me ever since. In business, in relationships, in everything—being a stranger in a strange land is the best education you can get. It teaches you humility. It teaches you patience. It teaches you that your way isn't the only way, and often isn't even the best way. As a result of London, I became more curious about other cultures. More willing to ask questions instead of making assumptions. More comfortable being the outsider, knowing that discomfort was the price of growth.

### Nancy

I met Nancy in a grocery store in Michigan, on one of those trips home between flight test rotations. I was standing near the eggs—I remember that detail with absurd clarity, the way you remember the trivial things that frame the moments that change your life—when I noticed the woman next to me, studying the price tag with an expression of genuine outrage.

"Can you believe these prices?" I said, because I had to say something. "Eggs are up, what, a hundred percent?"

She looked at me. Not the quick glance of polite dismissal, but a real look, appraising and amused. "You're not from here," she said. It wasn't a question.

"How can you tell?"

"The eggs," she said, deadpan. "Only an out-of-towner starts a conversation about eggs."

I laughed. She laughed. And something in that shared laugh felt different from the usual small talk of strangers—like the beginning of a conversation neither of us wanted to end. We talked for a few minutes, standing there in the dairy aisle like we had nowhere else to be. She was sharp. Quick. Her eyes saw more than you wanted them to see, but the way she looked at me wasn't unkind. Then we went our separate ways, and I spent the next three days kicking myself for not asking for her number.

A few days later, I was swimming laps in the apartment complex pool—where I was staying during my Michigan visits—and I saw a woman walk into the rental office. Familiar. The posture. The way she moved. I pulled myself out of the water, dripping, and walked over. She turned around. It was Nancy. She was there to pay her rent. She lived in the same building.

"What are the odds?" I said.

"In a town this size?" she replied. "Pretty good, actually. But I'll pretend to be surprised."

I asked her out. She said yes.

I remembered my mother's advice: "You don't have to be the smartest person in the room, Bobby. You just have to be the most real. People remember that."

So I tried to be real. On our first date—a diner with good pie and bad coffee—I asked her about herself. She worked at a bank in the trust department, but what she really wanted was to write. Novels, maybe. Stories, definitely. Her eyes lit up when she talked about it in a way they didn't when she talked about trusts and estates. Her ex-fiancé had called her literary ambitions frivolous. When she told me that, I saw a shadow cross her face—old hurt, still healing.

"That's not frivolous," I said. "Creating something out of words, making people feel things—that's harder than anything I've ever done."

She looked at me for a long moment. "You mean that."

"I do."

### Courtship

The second date was easier. The third was comfortable. By the fourth, we were finishing each other's sentences, laughing at jokes no one else would understand—that particular intimacy that emerges when two people recognize in each other something they didn't know they were seeking. I told her about my family: the father who didn't always know how to be soft, the mother who taught me to see past the yelling. Nancy told me about her failed engagement, the man who had wanted her to be someone she wasn't, who had seen her writing as a hobby rather than a calling.

There was a moment I still carry with me. We were walking through a park near her apartment, late autumn, leaves piled gold and red along the path. She stopped to look at a maple tree, branches almost bare against a gray Michigan sky. "I used to think I knew what my life would look like," she said quietly. "A house. A husband. A writing desk by a window. But the house and the husband were the wrong ones. The desk was the only part I got right." She turned to me. "What do you think your life looks like?"

I didn't have an answer. Not a good one. But the question stayed with me, and the fact that she asked it—that she wanted to know—told me more about who she was than any biography could. She wasn't looking for a man to complete her picture. She was looking for someone to share the blank page.

The night before I had to fly back to Florida, we sat in her apartment drinking wine and listening to a jazz station on the radio. I looked at her across the small table, lamplight catching the curve of her face, the way she tapped her fingers in time with the music, and I knew. Not with my head. With something deeper. The kind of knowing that doesn't need proof.

"This is going to be a long-distance thing for a while," I said. "Are you okay with that?"

She took a sip of her wine. "I'm okay with it if you are."

"I'm more than okay with it."

### Building a Life

We were married in the spring, a small ceremony in Michigan with Nancy's family and my parents making awkward small talk across the cultural divide that separated their worlds. My father stood stiff in his good suit, looking uncomfortable but proud. My mother cried, as mothers do. Nancy wore a simple white dress and looked at me like I was the only person in the room.

We bought a small house in Michigan with me commuting to Florida. It was the first time either of us had lived with another adult in a romantic partnership, and the learning curve was steep. I had to adjust to sharing space, to considering another person's preferences, to the give-and-take of domestic life. Nancy had to adjust to my long hours, my tendency to become absorbed in technical problems, my occasional withdrawal when work was frustrating. We fought, as all couples do. About small things—whose turn it was to do dishes, whether to spend money on new furniture or save for the future. About larger things—whether I was working too much, whether Nancy was too quick to accommodate my schedule at the expense of her own needs.

What I remember most from those early years was the feeling of partnership. When I succeeded at work, Nancy celebrated with me, understood why it mattered, made my victories feel real. When I struggled, she offered perspective, reminded me that my worth wasn't measured by professional achievement, held me when the weight of expectation felt overwhelming. And I tried to do the same for her.

"You're allowed to be obsessed with your work," Nancy told me once, after I apologized for talking about a technical problem through dinner. "I just need to know that I'm also important. That when it really matters, you'll be there."

"You matter more than the work," I said. "I sometimes forget to show it. But you matter more."

### The First Home

We bought our first house—a modest ranch in Michigan, close enough to the airport for my commute but in a town with good schools and a growing community. The house needed work. I approached it as an engineering project, creating plans, working weekends to transform the place into something we could be proud of.

"This is what my life has taught me," I said one Sunday evening, sitting on our newly finished deck with beers in hand, admiring the work. "Not just the skills, but the feeling. Making something better. Building something together."

"I understand now," Nancy said. "Why you love this. It's creation, but it's creation you can touch. Not like my writing, which is just words on paper. This is real."

I looked at her in the fading light of that summer evening and saw the contentment in her face. Felt the connection between us that had grown stronger with each challenge we had faced together. We were young, then, and optimistic, and in love. We believed we had time—time to build careers, raise children, achieve dreams, grow old together. We didn't know how little time we actually had, how quickly the future we were building would be changed by forces we couldn't anticipate. But that knowledge was still years away.

In 1975, on our deck, surrounded by the evidence of our competence and commitment, we were happy. The work was good. The marriage was strong. The future was bright with possibility.

I thought of my parents then, of all the lessons they had given me without knowing they were teaching. Measure twice, cut once. Build things that last. The house was just wood and wire and plumbing. The marriage was the real construction project, the thing we were building together day by day, choice by choice, through the ordinary challenges of shared life.

*But life, as I was about to learn, has a way of building foundations just to test whether they can hold.*
